summary: Defines how to carry NETCONF messages over SOAP, an XML messaging format common in web services, so existing web-service tools can manage devices. This RFC is historic.

eli5.summary: NETCONF is a way to give instructions to network machines. This note wrapped those instructions in an envelope style used by websites. People stopped using the idea, so it is now historic.

subtitle: How to carry NETCONF configuration messages inside SOAP envelopes over HTTP or BEEP.

tldr.problem: NETCONF needed a way to be used from web-service environments, where SOAP and its tooling were the common way to exchange XML messages.
tldr.mechanism: Each NETCONF message is placed in the body of a SOAP envelope and sent over HTTP (or HTTPS) or BEEP, with a short WSDL describing the service and the NETCONF session tied to the transport connection.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is now Historic and was updated by RFC 8996, so it should not be treated as a current way to run NETCONF.

today: RFC 4743 is Historic and was updated by RFC 8996. The base protocol it binds to is described in RFC 4741, which is the NETCONF specification it cites.

sections.title: Why Put NETCONF in SOAP
sections.content:
RFC 4743 proposes a binding of NETCONF operations to SOAP, an XML messaging scheme. Both NETCONF and SOAP have a remote procedure call character, so SOAP is a natural fit. Two bindings are described: SOAP over HTTP and SOAP over BEEP (the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol).

The RFC admits the technical gain is modest: SOAP gives a standard envelope with a header and a body. The practical reason is stronger. SOAP over HTTP with WSDL is supported by many tools and operating systems and understood by many developers, which helps a device management protocol get implemented and adopted. The RFC concedes there are interoperability problems with SOAP and WSDL, but expects them to be resolved. It calls the short WSDL document in Section 3.7 the most important part, because with the base NETCONF XML schemas it gives a machine-readable description for building software.
sections.eli5: Lots of tools already know how to open a certain kind of envelope, so the authors decided to put NETCONF letters inside that envelope.

sections.title: HTTP, BEEP and BCP 56
sections.content:
SOAP over HTTP is what most SOAP software supports. HTTP has awkward points: the client always starts the connection, so server-initiated data and notifications are hard; headers are verbose; idle connections may be closed by proxies; and bulk transfer relies on stream-based ordering. The RFC judges these are not fatal for device management. SOAP over BEEP is called technically superior, because either peer can start an exchange, but it is not as widely adopted.

It also takes up the concerns in BCP 56 (RFC 3205) about using HTTP as a substrate. HTTP caches SHOULD NOT sit between managers and agents, because NETCONF session state is tied to the transport connection. The defences are to forbid caching with the Cache-Control and Pragma: no-cache headers, to keep HTTP proxies out of the management network, and to use HTTPS. HTTP persistent connections and chunked transfer-coding SHOULD be used.
sections.eli5: Mail carried by the old route only lets the sender start a conversation. The memo explains why that is good enough and how to avoid the main traps.

sections.title: Sessions Over SOAP
sections.content:
A manager (a management console) opens an HTTP or BEEP connection to an agent on a device and drives the NETCONF session with a series of SOAP messages. The session starts when the first SOAP message is POSTed to the NETCONF web application URI (HTTP) or when the BEEP SOAP profile handshake sets up the channel. Closing the connection or channel ends the session.

Capabilities are exchanged with <hello> messages. Over HTTP the client MUST send the first <hello>; BEEP has no ordering constraint. The agent assigns the session ID. Session state covers authentication, capabilities, locks, pending operations and operation sequence numbers, and locks are released when the session ends.

NETCONF over SOAP makes little use of SOAP features. Operations are not split into message parts and the SOAP header is not used, a deliberate choice so the same messages can be handled over several substrates.
sections.eli5: The manager knocks, both sides swap lists of what they can do, and the machine gives the visit a number. When the door closes, the visit is over.

sections.title: Faults and the WSDL
sections.content:
When NETCONF returns an <rpc-error>, a SOAP Fault wraps it so SOAP software can turn it into a language-level exception. The Fault Code Value is Receiver in the SOAP envelope namespace, the Fault Reason Text is the contents of the error-tag, and the Fault detail is the original <rpc-error>.

The WSDL in Section 3.7 declares two operations, hello and rpc, using the document style with literal bodies. A <get-config> request is therefore simply a SOAP envelope whose body holds the usual <rpc>, and the reply holds <rpc-reply>. Section 3.8 shows a sample service definition that a device would publish to give its own address.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, the error note is tucked inside a standard complaint form so ordinary web software knows what to do with it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NETCONF reads and changes configuration, so access should be limited to authorized users and systems. Both sides should be authenticated, and because configuration can include user names or keys, NETCONF should only run over channels with strong encryption.

The binding relies on a secure transport such as TLS (HTTPS when combined with HTTP) or IPsec. Authentication can happen in the transport, in HTTP (for example Digest), or in SOAP. Implementations MUST support TLS: NETCONF over SOAP over HTTP MUST support HTTPS, and over BEEP MUST support BEEP over TLS. The RFC notes that an authorization model is not currently specified for NETCONF, and that unencrypted transports may suit closed networks or debugging but are vulnerable.
sections.eli5: Because these messages can change how a machine works, they need a locked, private channel and a check that both sides are who they say they are.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned TCP port 833 for NETCONF over SOAP over BEEP and TCP port 832 for NETCONF over SOAP over HTTPS. Conforming implementations MUST default to attempting connections on this new standard port, and the assigned port SHOULD be used because it allows efficient firewall filtering during possible denial-of-service attacks.

The memo also asks for an XML namespace for the WSDL definitions, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:soap, under the "Specification Required" policy.
sections.eli5: The memo got its own numbered doorways on the network so nobody has to share the busy front door of the web.
